query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the Mo content with an equivalent atomic percent of Nb in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will lower its density without sacrificing its high‐temperature and room‐temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast high entropy alloy composed of Hf, Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ that exhibits high strength at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Substitute Mo with Nb on an equiatomic basis, i.e. producing an alloy with composition HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing under both room temperature and elevated temperature conditions (~1000 °C), subjected to tensile and creep loading regimes similar to those in the original alloy's applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the high entropy, disordered solid solution structure. The similar atomic radii and bonding environment between Mo and Nb should preserve lattice distortion and dislocation behavior that underpin the strength and creep resistance.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a lower atomic mass (atomic weight ~93) than Mo (atomic weight ~96), so replacing Mo with Nb is expected to lower the overall alloy density. Because Nb has similar metallurgical characteristics to Mo in high entropy systems, the substitution should minimally affect the microstructural stability and strength mechanisms at both room and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy (HfNbTaTiZr) will exhibit a reduced density (potentially lowering the density by approximately 5–7%, near values reported for related alloys) while retaining comparable yield strength and creep resistance at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with its current density and mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies when Mo is substituted by Nb at equivalently high percentages so that the high entropy effects and associated microstructural stability remain intact; effects outside the temperature range of room temperature to approximately 1000 °C or significant changes in processing are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of density reduction and the degree to which high‐temperature mechanical properties are fully preserved remain to be quantitatively verified. There is some uncertainty regarding possible microstructural changes induced by the substitution that could affect long‐term performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the control as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy and (b) the Nb‐substituted variant HfNbTaTiZr using similar processing and homogenization methods. Assess the density of both alloys and conduct standardized tensile and creep tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at room temperature and 1000 °C
Creep rate measurements under comparable loads
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloy does not display a statistically significant reduction in density (e.g., less than a 5% decrease) or if its mechanical properties (yield strength, creep resistance) at room temperature and ~1000 °C are significantly lower than those of the original HfMoTaTiZr alloy, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. Among the various systems of alloying elements studied, the Ta 20 Nb 20 Hf 20 Zr 20 Ti 20 alloy seems to be attractive due to its reduced density of 9.94 g/cm 3 [ [2] , [3] ], few publications [ [4] , [5] , [6] ] deal with thr thermodynamic properties of certain compositions of the Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti.
